articles.title: Association of Dysphagia Risk and Nutritional Status with Caregiver Burden and Quality of Life in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that leads to significant functional decline, including dysphagia and malnutrition. These complications not only affect disease progression but may also influence caregiver well-being. However, studies simultaneously examining the associations among dysphagia risk, nutritional status, caregiver burden, and caregiver quality of life remain limited, particularly in Türkiye. This study aimed to investigate the associations of dysphagia risk and nutritional status with disease severity, caregiver burden, and caregiver quality of life in individuals with ALS. This cross-sectional study included 60 individuals diagnosed with ALS and their 60 primary caregivers, recruited through an ALS association's social media platforms. Assessments were conducted online via videoconferencing. Disease severity was evaluated using the ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R). Dysphagia risk was screened using the Eating Assessment Tool (EAT-10;cut-off ≥3), and nutritional status was assessed using the Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA). Caregiver burden was measured with the Zarit Caregiver Burden Scale (ZCBS), and caregiver quality of life was assessed using the Short Form-36 (SF-36). Multiple linear regression models adjusted for ALSFRS-R score, caregiver age, and caregiver sex were used to examine independent associations, with Holm and false discovery rate corrections for multiple comparisons. The mean ALSFRS-R score was 15.0 ± 12.6, indicating a predominantly advanced-stage sample. Fifty-one participants (85%) screened positive for dysphagia risk (EAT-10 ≥3). According to the MNA, 60% were malnourished and 30% were at risk of malnutrition. After adjustment for ALSFRS-R score, caregiver age, and caregiver sex, higher EAT-10 scores (β = 0.40, pHolm = 0.007) and lower MNA scores (β =-0.42, pHolm = 0.007) were independently associated with greater caregiver burden, each explaining 11-12% of additional variance, whereas ALSFRS-R score was no longer significantly associated with burden. Both variables were also independently associated with caregiver vitality, mental health, bodily pain, and general health (q < 0.05). Dysphagia risk and poorer nutritional status in individuals with ALS were associated with greater caregiver burden and reduced caregiver quality of life independently of overall disease severity. However, these associations should be interpreted cautiously given the cross-sectional design and the predominantly advanced-stage sample. These findings suggest that routine dysphagia screening and nutritional monitoring within multidisciplinary ALS care may be relevant not only for patient management but also for supporting caregiver well-being. Longitudinal studies using dysphagia-specific caregiver measures are needed to clarify the direction of these associations.

articles.title: Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 participates in the internalization of arginine-rich dipeptide repeat proteins.
articles.abstract: Microsatellite repeat expansion of the 5' GGGGCC 3' sequence in the C9orf72 gene is the most common monogenic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. Dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) translated from the mutant allele can be detected in postmortem brains of afflicted individuals. The arginine containing peptides, poly proline-arginine (poly-PR) and poly glycine-arginine (poly-GR), are particularly noxious to cells. Both can undergo cell-to-cell transmission, but underlying mechanisms are not understood. We found rapid internalization and nucleolar localization of bath-applied hemagglutinin (HA) tagged poly-PR with twenty repeats (HA-PR 20 ) in cell lines and neurons. Small molecule and RNAi approaches implicated a temperature-dependent, fluid phase endocytosis mechanism for HA-PR 20 . We sought to identify DPR-related cell surface uptake factors using µMap high-resolution proximity labeling. DPR-iridium conjugates identified candidate cell-surface proteins which were interrogated in a secondary RNAi screen. Focusing on our strongest candidate, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 (CSPG4), we showed cellular uptake of HA-PR 20 is reduced by inhibition of glycosaminoglycan chain synthesis and knockdown or ablation of CSPG4. Knockdown of CSPG4 protected PR 20 -induced neuronal toxicity. Using a dual reporter system to interrogate in vitro neuron-to-neuron transmission of PR 50, we found PR 50 synthesized by one neuron readily spread to neighboring cells. Transmission was significantly reduced with CSPG4 knockdown. Similarly conditioned media from PR 50 or GR 50 expressing neurons contained transmissible protein that was internalized into neurons in a CSPG4-dependent manner. These results suggest CSPG4 participates in poly-PR/poly-GR internalization and transmission.

articles.title: Expanding Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Genetic Spectrum via Systematic Screening of Adult-Onset Neurologic Disease Genes.
articles.abstract: Emerging evidence indicates that amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) shares genetic architecture with other neurologic disorders, whose causal variants may be overlooked by targeted sequencing. Here, we evaluated the occurrence of pathogenic variants in genes linked to adult-onset neurologic disorders among individuals with ALS. Short-read WGS was performed in retrospectively collected ALS (Gold Coast criteria) and primary lateral sclerosis (PLS) (consensus diagnostic criteria) patients consecutively recruited at an Italian tertiary referral center (2013-2023), extensively phenotyped to exclude mimics. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic single-nucleotide variants/indels (American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines) and short tandem repeat expansions across 453 genes, including established ALS genes and other neurodegenerative disease genes, were systematically screened and validated. C9orf72 expansions (>30 repeats) were routinely screened by fragment analysis and repeat-primed PCR. A total of 856 patients with ALS and PLS (median age at onset 61.8 years, 38.5% women) were enrolled. Among them, 168 (19.6%) carried pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants or short tandem repeat expansions in genes associated with adult-onset neurologic disorders, mostly autosomal dominant. Of these, 41 (4.8% of the cohort) harbored variants in non-ALS/frontotemporal dementia (FTD) genes (ataxias, neuropathies, myopathies, movement disorders, mitochondrial diseases, and hereditary spastic paraplegia [HSP]). Repeat expansions accounted for 11.9% of cases, while 0.6% carried both sequence variants and repeat expansions. Family history of ALS/FTD ( p = 2.132e-06), other neurodegenerative disorders ( p = 0.0006934), and earlier age at onset ( p = 0.024) were enriched among variant carriers. Variants in genes associated with upper motor neuron (UMN) involvement (ataxias/HSP) did not predict an UMN-predominant phenotype (odds ratio 1.54, 95% CI 0.39-6.07, p = 0.54), while the association between neuropathy/myopathy genes and a lower motor neuron-predominant phenotype was not statistically estimable. Beyond established ALS pathways, enrichment was observed in mitochondrial, metabolic, and proteostasis pathways (false discovery rate ≤0.05). Although the absence of a control cohort limits assessment of variant enrichment, the identification of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in genes associated with adult-onset neurologic disorders other than ALS/FTD in patients with ALS supports the inclusion of broader gene panels to advance precision medicine in ALS.

articles.title: Robustness of Plasma P-Tau217 Diagnostic Thresholds for Alzheimer Disease Across Various Clinical Populations and Laboratory Environments.
articles.abstract: Blood-based biomarkers (BBMs), especially plasma tau phosphorylated at threonine 217 (p-tau217), could scale Alzheimer disease (AD) clinical-biological diagnosis, but clinical use requires thresholds transferable across laboratories and populations. We compared Lumipulse p-tau217 with other BBMs; evaluated amyloid-anchored thresholds across centers, analyzers, reagent lots, and clinical populations; and assessed second-line CSF adjudication of gray zone results. This multicenter, cross-sectional diagnostic-classification study included an exploratory Brussels cohort and 3 external validation cohorts. Brussels participants were cognitively unimpaired or impaired and had Aβ status determined by amyloid-PET or CSF Aβ42 and tau status by tau-PET or CSF p-tau181. Validation cohorts comprised consecutive Paris memory-clinic patients, patients with early-onset neurodegenerative dementia in Bordeaux, and individuals with monogenic frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). Plasma p-tau217 was measured locally on Lumipulse analyzers. BBMs and ratios were compared using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. In Brussels, a Youden cutoff and dual 95% or 97.5% sensitivity/specificity cutoffs were derived; intermediate values defined gray zones. Among 411 participants (mean age 70.5 years; 51.6% female), p-tau217 showed the best diagnostic performance; p-tau217/Aβ42 did not improve performance or reduce gray zones. In Brussels, p-tau217 discriminated Aβ+ from Aβ- status (AUC 0.96, 95% CI 0.93-0.98; p < 0.0001). The 0.193 pg/mL Youden cutoff (95% CI 0.178-0.213) yielded 91.5% sensitivity (95% CI 84.7-95.5) and 91.6% specificity (95% CI 84.8-95.5) and detected neocortical tau-PET positivity with 98.5% sensitivity and 81.8% specificity. In Paris, sensitivity/specificity for clinical-biological AD were 93.2% (95% CI 85.1-97.1)/93.0% (95% CI 81.4-97.6); in Bordeaux, sensitivity/specificity for clinical-biological AD were 95.7% (95% CI 79.0-99.2)/92.3% (95% CI 66.7-98.6). Specificity in monogenic FTLD was 88.4% (95% CI 75.5-94.9). False-positive classifications were enriched in FTLD with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Dual thresholds yielded gray zones in 15.4%-24.8% of Paris patients; second-line CSF testing resolved 86.2%-88.9% of gray zone cases. Lumipulse plasma p-tau217 thresholds were transferable across centers, analyzers, reagent lots, and heterogeneous clinical populations, supporting evaluation of plasma-first pathways with confirmatory testing for gray zone values. Values below 0.193 pg/mL made neocortical tauopathy unlikely. Limitations include cross-sectional design, specialized Western European recruitment, unavailable race/ethnicity data, heterogeneous reference standards, incomplete AD copathology adjudication in monogenic FTLD, and no cross-platform comparison.

articles.title: Taurine metabolism: a potential target for neuroprotection in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.
articles.abstract: Taurine is one of the most abundant free amino acids in mammals and plays essential roles in cellular homeostasis, mitochondrial function, calcium regulation and neuronal survival. Taurine availability varies markedly across tissues, species and sexes, reflecting the balance between endogenous synthesis, dietary intake, transport and efflux. Although reduced taurine levels have been reported in some aging tissues, recent longitudinal studies indicate that circulating taurine does not decline universally with age, and its value as a biomarker of aging remains debated. Alterations in taurine or its transporter SLC6A6 have been described in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease and retinal degenerations. Preclinical studies indicate that taurine supplementation mitigates excitotoxicity, stabilizes mitochondrial function, reduces neuroinflammation and supports myelination and synaptic balance. Despite this strong mechanistic rationale, clinical evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, underscoring the need for biomarker-guided trials and a clearer definition of optimal therapeutic windows. In this review, we summarize the general properties of taurine and its metabolic regulation. We examine taurine's neuroprotective properties across different neurodegenerative conditions and discuss future perspectives for targeting taurine metabolism as a promising but largely unexplored strategy for intervention in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.

articles.title: Tofersen in the treatment of SOD1 ALS - a two-year experience from the Polish Early Access Program.
articles.abstract: The use of tofersen, an antisense oligonucleotide against SOD1, has been recommended for the treatment of SOD1-ALS by current European guidelines. Before full approval by national health funding agencies, patients received tofersen through the Early Access Program (EAP) and/or as rescue therapy. The aim of the study was to prospectively analyze clinical outcomes and neurofilament light chain (NfL) concentration in patients participating in the EAP in Poland between October 2023 and October 2025. Twenty patients with SOD1-ALS (11 with familial and 9 with sporadic ALS; male:female ratio, 2.2:1) were enrolled in the EAP. They carried 11 SOD1 pathological variants, the most frequent being L145S and K4E. As 1 patient withdrew after the first dose of treatment, data were collected from 19 individuals. The median age at disease onset was 49 years (33-69 years). Disease duration before treatment was 39 months (8-110 months), and the median age at initiation of tofersen treatment was 51 years (39-74 years). The analysis included demographic and genetic data, ALS functional rating scale-revised (ALSFRS- -R), ALS progression rate, forced vital capacity (FVC), adverse events, and NfL concentration in cerebrospinal fluid. The median duration of tofersen treatment was 16 months (7-24 months). ALSFRS-R stabilized or increased in 68% of cases. Median delta ALSFRS-R during the treatment period was 0/month. The overall median progression rate decreased significantly from 0.218/month before treatment to 0.145/month at the last assessment (p < 0.0001). The decrease was observed in all patients, including fast-progressing individuals with continuous functional decline, as well as those with the most benign disease course. Two patients developed respiratory insufficiency, while FVC did not deteriorate in the remaining subjects. NfL concentration decreased in all analyzed patients, with significant reductions after 9 and 14 months. Serious treatment-related adverse events (SAEs) occurred in 3 patients and resolved without clinical consequences in 2 individuals. Two patients died due to disease progression and/or exacerbation of a preexisting condition/SAE. The long-term follow-up data support the clinical efficacy and acceptable safety profile of tofersen treatment and demonstrate a biomarker response reflecting reduced axonal injury in both slow- and fast-progressing SOD1-ALS.

articles.title: [Factors influencing family decision-making regarding autopsy in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis].
articles.abstract: This study aimed to identify factors influencing family decision-making regarding autopsy in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Semi-structured interviews were conducted with bereaved family members of 12 deceased patients with ALS, and the data were analyzed using a qualitative descriptive approach. Autopsy was performed in 8 of the 12 cases. Seven factors influencing decision-making for autopsy were identified: prosocial motivation, meaning-making, patient preferences, family dynamics, trust in healthcare professionals, decision-making constraints, and disease-related context. Families perceived autopsy as contributing to medical research, reflecting the patient's wishes, and providing support for the bereaved, while also experiencing conflict and emotional burden. Decision-making regarding autopsy in ALS is shaped by interactions between value-based factors and contextual factors. Sharing patient preferences in advance may help reduce the burden associated with decision-making among bereaved family members.

articles.title: Cholesterol dysmetabolism in motor neurons drives ALS pathogenesis.
articles.abstract: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), cholesterol dysmetabolism in motor neurons has emerged as a central pathogenic axis. Oxysterols generated under oxidative stress exert potent lower motor neuron toxicity via lysosomal and mitochondrial dysfunction and by triggering oxiapoptophagy, a form of cell death in which oxidative stress, apoptosis, and autophagy co-occur. Moreover, TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) dysfunction and pathogenic variants in ALS-related genes including C9orf72, VAPB, and SIGMAR1 can amplify lipid toxicity through impaired function of mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum membranes (MAMs) and defective intracellular cholesterol trafficking. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses indicate that genetically predicted elevations in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), total cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B (ApoB) are associated with increased ALS risk, whereas the effects of statins appear heterogeneous and context-dependent, varying by agent, dose, and treatment duration. In drug discovery using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived lower motor neurons (iPSC-LMNs), ropinirole hydrochloride suppresses the expression of enzymes involved in de novo cholesterol synthesis while reducing reactive oxygen species, inhibiting aggregation of TDP-43 and fused in sarcoma (FUS), and improving mitochondrial function; importantly, in vitro responsiveness correlates with clinical efficacy. Furthermore, integrating a polygenic risk score (PRS) for total cholesterol with iPSC-LMN phenotypes has been proposed as a stratification strategy to define an ALS subtype driven by hyperactive cholesterol metabolism and to identify patients more likely to benefit from cholesterol biosynthesis-suppressing therapies. Collectively, candidate disease-modifying interventions targeting cholesterol dysmetabolism are increasingly positioned as a promising translational research axis in ALS.

articles.title: Guam disease features chronic traumatic encephalopathy-like tau seeds in brain and spinal cord.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/parkinsonism-dementia complex (ALS/PDC) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder that was once hyperendemic in the island of Guam (Mariana Islands, US) and a few other Pacific locales. Despite extensive investigations into its origins, the etiology of ALS/PDC remains unclear. ALS/PDC is, at the neuropathology level, characterized by tau-dominant multiple proteinopathy in brain and spinal cord. It was recently reported that Guam ALS/PDC brain extracts exhibit tau seeding activity in fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based biosensor cells. To build upon those findings and explore the nature of tau seeds in ALS/PDC in more detail, we used an alanine mutational scanning (Ala scan) approach to determine the seeding profile of tau in nervous tissues of Guam ALS/PDC cases. First, we confirmed the detection of tau seeding activity in ALS/PDC brain samples in tau biosensor cells. Notably, we could also detect potent tau seeding activity in spinal cord. Subsequent Ala scan assays demonstrated that ALS/PDC tau displays an aggregate incorporation pattern that resembles that of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE)-type tau. This result is consistent with recent electron cryo-microscopy studies of tau, which revealed that ALS/PDC tau filaments are predominantly of the CTE-type. The structural characteristics and seeding behaviour of ALS/PDC tau, as well as the regional distribution of tau pathology at post-mortem, suggest that ALS/PDC is a CTE-like tauopathy.

articles.title: Neuropharmacology of omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids in neurodegenerative diseases: mechanisms, multi-omics evidence, and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, involve progressive neuronal dysfunction associated with neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial impairment, defective proteostasis, and synaptic failure. Although symptomatic treatment remains central, anti-amyloid therapies can modestly slow clinical decline in selected patients with early Alzheimer's disease. This review critically evaluates the neuropharmacological evidence for omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, particularly docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), and the barriers to their clinical translation. We narratively synthesized preclinical, observational, and interventional clinical evidence, focusing on membrane organization, inflammatory resolution, mitochondrial and redox homeostasis, autophagy, proteostasis, neuronal signaling, and factors contributing to heterogeneous clinical outcomes. Preclinical studies support context-dependent effects of DHA and EPA on neuronal membranes, inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial function, redox balance, autophagy, and synaptic plasticity. Human evidence is less consistent: observational studies generally report favorable associations between omega-3 status and neurological outcomes, whereas randomized trials show null, modest, or subgroup-dependent effects. Outcomes vary with disease stage, baseline omega-3 status, formulation, dose, treatment duration, genotype, and endpoint selection. Uncertain central nervous system exposure and limited pharmacokinetic and target-engagement data remain major translational barriers. Omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids are biologically plausible neuropharmacological modulators, but current evidence does not establish DHA or EPA as broadly effective disease-modifying treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. Future trials should prioritize early-stage, biomarker-stratified populations, pharmacologically characterized formulations, adequate treatment duration, and clinically meaningful progression-related outcomes.

articles.title: Power-law age-dependence supports phenotype-specific multistep architecture in MND.
articles.abstract: To determine whether age-specific motor neuron disease (MND) incidence is better described by power-law age-dependence, compatible with multistep architecture, or by an exponential model. We analyzed curated Australian Motor Neuron Disease Registry data using age at symptom onset, clinical phenotype and Australian population denominators. The primary analysis modeled age-specific incidence across the 30-75-year range using 5-year age bands. Power-law and exponential Poisson models were compared using differences in Akaike Information Criterion (ΔAIC), with supplementary analyses across an expanded 20-90-year range and a restricted younger age range (<60 years). Across 2,556 patients in the primary analysis, the power-law model provided superior fit to the exponential model in the total cohort, with a ΔAIC of 60.06. The estimated power-law slope was 3.75, corresponding to 4.75 apparent steps. Power-law superiority was observed across clinical phenotypes, with the highest apparent step estimates in bulbar-onset ALS and flail arm syndrome, and the lowest in cervical-onset ALS and primary lateral sclerosis. Sensitivity analyses across expanded and restricted age ranges supported the primary findings. In the Australian MND Registry cohort, power-law age-dependence provided a better fit to observed age-specific incidence than the exponential alternative. These findings are compatible with a multistep model of MND pathogenesis but do not establish a fixed sequence of discrete pathogenic events.

articles.title: Breathing in an Accelerated World: Temporality, Ethical Repertoires, and Medical Students' Examination Texts on Advanced Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Medical students are commonly examined on ethically difficult clinical decisions, yet examination scripts have rarely been treated as a distinct empirical object in medical humanities. This article analyses 61 anonymised written examination responses from Danish medical students addressing acute respiratory failure in a fictional patient with advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The study is framed as a genre analysis of examination texts, operationalised through repeated close reading, inductive coding of recurrent textual moves, and abductive interpretation through Hartmut Rosa's concepts of acceleration and resonance. Four ethical repertoires were identified: accelerated stabilisation; prognostic triage and the limit of intervention; distributed responsibility and the search for a legitimate pause; and fragile resonance through attention to wishes, dignity, and palliative alternatives. Across the corpus, students wrote judgement through temporal distinctions between urgency and delay, reversibility and progression, and escalation and proportionate limitation. The findings do not show professionalism as such, but rather the institutionally legitimate ways in which professional judgement is made legible under assessment. Examination scripts matter for medical humanities because they make curricular normativity and evaluative pressure textually visible, showing how future clinicians are taught to write responsibility, uncertainty, and care into the same ethical scene. These repertoires also render an ableist prognostic imagination institutionally legible-one in which ventilator-dependent life is readily scripted in advance as a future to be avoided rather than supported-linking the temporal analysis to critical disability studies' account of the curative imaginary.

articles.title: Health-Related Quality of Life Across Neurologic Conditions: A Cross-Sectional Cohort Study Using Real-World Patient-Reported Outcomes.
articles.abstract: Health-related quality of life (HRQOL) is an important outcome within value-based care for patients with neurologic conditions. The American Academy of Neurology recommends the use of Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Global Health as a patient-reported outcome performance measure to assess stability or improvement over 1 year. However, interpretation of this measure requires an understanding of HRQOL across neurologic populations. Our study leveraged real-world data collected through the electronic health record to characterize differences in HRQOL across common neurologic conditions. This is a cross-sectional study of adult patients with 1 of 10 conditions (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis [ALS], back pain, brain tumor, dementia, major depression, epilepsy, migraine, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease, and stroke) who completed patient-reported outcomes as standard care between October 2015 and March 2023 at a large Neurologic Institute. Patients completed PROMIS-GH, from which physical and mental summary scores (Global Mental Health [GMH], Global Physical Health [GPH]) were calculated, PHQ-9 depression screen, and condition-specific measures. EQ-5D utility index was estimated from PROMIS-GH. These were summarized across conditions after adjustment for demographics, clinical characteristics, and self-reported condition-specific severity. There were 133,636 patients included in this analysis (mean age 51.5 [SD ± 18] years, 64% female, 81% White race). Overall adjusted average scores for GPH, GMH, PHQ-9, and EQ-5D were 42.7 ± 5.0, 43.6 ± 5.0, 7.9 ± 3.7, and 0.68 ± 0.11, respectively. Scores were significantly different across condition, with GPH ranging from 39.6 ± 5.5 for back pain to 45.9 ± 3.9 for brain tumor. Patients with brain tumor, back pain, stroke, ALS, and multiple sclerosis had more favorable GMH and PHQ-9 scores, while patients with depression, epilepsy, and dementia had the most affected GMH and PHQ-9 scores. Patients with back pain and headache had the lowest EQ-5D scores (0.63 ± 0.13 and 0.67 ± 0.09), while those with brain tumor had the highest (0.77 ± 0.08). This study provides condition-specific and severity-specific benchmarks for PROMIS-GH and related HRQOL measures that can support interpretation of patient-reported outcomes across neurologic populations. These data inform clinical care, quality measurement, research, and the implementation of the AAN-recommended performance measure.

articles.title: iPSC-based Approaches to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: from Drug Screening to Regenerative Medicine in Early Clinical Translation.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterised by progressive loss of upper and lower motor neurons (MNs), with limited therapeutic options and modest benefit from currently approved drugs. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have emerged as a versatile platform for ALS research, enabling both regenerative medicine and phenotypic drug screening. iPSC-based transplantation strategies aim to replace lost cells or deliver neuroprotective support, while iPSC-derived MNs support drug discovery and repositioning. In the two decades since their discovery, iPSC technologies have progressed from concept to clinical translation, with both cell therapy products such as AstroRx and XS-228 entering trials and three screened drug candidates, Ropinirole, Bosutinib, and Ezogabine, advancing into clinical trials, underscoring their translational potential. In this review, we summarise iPSC-based approaches to ALS, focusing on cell therapies and drug discovery, highlight factors influencing transplantation success, and discuss ongoing clinical trials. We further discuss constraints that impede clinical trial progress, including limited understanding of ALS pathogenesis, absence of robust biomarkers to guide patient stratification and evaluate treatment response, and technical challenges related to the maturation of iPSC-derived neural cells. Finally, we advocate that advancing iPSC approaches requires both deeper understanding of ALS biology and technical innovation. Key priorities are refining iPSC differentiation protocols to improve neuronal maturity and implementing trial designs with adequate duration and rigorous patient stratification.

articles.title: Sphingolipid remodeling in SPT-related neuropathies.
articles.abstract: Sphingolipid homeostasis is critical for structural and functional integrity of neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems. Serine-palmitoyltransferase (SPT) is the first and the rate-limiting metabolic entry point into the de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis. Mutations in SPT subunits, SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 lead to contrasting patient phenotypes, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1 (HSAN1). A third mixed sensory-motor phenotype is attributed to distinct mutation sets in SPTLC1 and SPTLC2. However, a direct comparison of the metabolic consequences of mutations spanning these disease conditions has not been performed. Here, we demonstrate that SPTLC1- and SPTLC2-ALS variants contribute to enhanced sphingolipid synthesis as the ceramide-mediated homeostatic control is impaired. In contrast, HSAN1 variants display altered substrate selectivity, favoring non-canonical 1-deoxysphingolipid production while retaining canonical feedback regulation. Mixed sensory-motor mutants exhibit a third metabolic state, with elevated 1-deoxysphingolipid formation and, in contrast to HSAN1 variants, decreased feedback inhibition and increased canonical sphingolipid synthesis. Sphingolipid profiling reveals that ALS variants are characterized by preferential accumulation of dihydrosphingolipids and sphingolipid species containing C 18 -C 22 N-acyl chains, whereas very-long-chain (C 22 -C 26 ) 1-deoxysphingolipids predominate in HSAN1. The SPT-variants associated with mixed sensory-motor symptoms show elevated levels of both lipid types. Notably, the metabolic distinction is disease-specific and SPT subunit independent. The data support the view that segregated shifts in sphingolipid flux underlie divergence of clinical phenotypes in SPT-variants. These metabolic configurations generate testable predictions for therapy: L-serine supplementation may benefit HSAN1 but could prove counterproductive in ALS and sensory-motor disease conditions.

articles.title: Thyroid Disease and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Thyroid disease has been implicated in the pathology of neurodegenerative diseases. However, its role in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is unclear. This study aimed to investigate the association between thyroid disease, including hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, and the risk of ALS. We used a matched cohort design to evaluate UK Biobank data on participants enrolled between 2006 and 2010 who were followed up until 2022. We used Cox proportional hazards models to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The study cohort comprised 42,684 patients with thyroid disease (females: 80%). Thyroid disease was moderately associated with an increased risk of ALS development (HR: 1.44, 95% CI: 1.02-2.02), and this association remained similar following adjustment for comparative height at the age of 10 years (HR: 1.44, 95% CI: 1.03-2.03). Hyperthyroidism showed a potential association with an increased risk of ALS development among individuals aged ≤60 years (HR: 21.22, 95% CI: 1.64-274.46) and in females (HR: 3.02, 95% CI: 1.13-8.08). Our findings demonstrate that thyroid disease is associated with a moderately increased risk of ALS development. Given the multifunctional role of the thyroid gland, further in-depth studies examining the relationship between thyroid conditions and ALS are warranted.

articles.title: Tongue ultrasonography as a quantitative biomarker for oropharyngeal dysphagia in neuromuscular disorders: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: Oropharyngeal Dysphagia (OD) is a prevalent and potentially life-threatening complication of Neuromuscular Disorders (NMDs). Tongue ultrasonography is an inexpensive, non-ionising, point-of-care technique that permits quantitative assessment of lingual muscle structure, but its value as a biomarker of OD across NMDs has not been systematically appraised. This systematic review aims to synthesize the available evidence on the diagnostic accuracy, reliability and clinical utility of quantitative tongue ultrasonography as a biomarker of OD in adults with NMDs. We systematically searched PubMed and Scopus for studies correlating quantitative tongue-ultrasound parameters, Tongue Thickness (TT) or Echo Intensity (EI), with instrumental swallowing assessment in adults with NMDs, following the PRISMA 2020 guideline. Study selection, data extraction and risk-of-bias appraisal were performed independently by two reviewers. Six studies (n = 10-38 per cohort) met the inclusion criteria. Reduced TT was a consistent marker of lingual atrophy in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and correlated with oral-phase swallowing impairment, whereas functional measures of tongue strength were stronger predictors of aspiration risk. In Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), increased TT reflected "pseudohypertrophy" from fatty and connective-tissue infiltration rather than preserved function and EI provided a complementary index of tissue quality in myopathic NMDs. Tongue ultrasonography is a promising, disease-sensitive biomarker for monitoring bulbar dysfunction in NMDs, but morphological indices should be integrated with functional swallowing data to predict aspiration risk. Standardized acquisition protocols and larger, longitudinal, multicentre studies are required before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Reconciling cryptic relatedness to drive gene discovery in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/frontotemporal dementia.
Rethinking Digital Outcome Measures for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Trials: Consensus Priorities for Actigraphy Harmonization, Validation, and Regulatory Readiness.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) clinical trials need outcome measures that complement established end points while capturing how people function in daily life. In this viewpoint, we draw on our collective experience in ALS research, clinical trials, digital-measure development, and regulatory science, together with published evidence, a preliminary patient survey, stakeholder discussions, and experience from multisite actigraphy studies. We argue that the field now has a substantial base of longitudinal data and candidate measures, but lacks the coordinated framework needed to compare, prioritize, and validate them across studies. We identify 4 linked priorities: adopt fit-for-purpose measures in stages and within defined contexts of use; harmonize data collection and analysis; use data to shortlist and validate measures across cohorts; and prepare actigraphy methods for trial adoption through early industry and regulatory engagement. Across these priorities, actigraphy should complement rather than replace established clinical outcomes, with its integration guided by patient relevance, ALS phenotypic heterogeneity, participant, and caregiver burden, and the intended context of use. Our central message is that progress now depends less on generating additional isolated datasets or measures than on coordinating the evaluation of existing assets, and aligning future evidence generation.

articles.title: The Boron-Neuron Connection: The Potential of Boron-Containing Molecules for Treating Incurable Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Boron (B), a group 13 metalloid, has emerged as a versatile element at the intersection of chemistry, biology, and medicine. Its electron-deficient nature and ability to reversibly interconvert between trigonal planar (sp 2 ) and tetrahedral (sp 3 ) geometries enable dynamic covalent interactions with biological nucleophiles, making boron-containing compounds (BCCs) attractive pharmacophores that selectively interact with reactive oxygen species (ROS) and are ROS-responsive for therapeutic development. BCCs possess antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and metal-chelating properties that make them attractive candidates for neurodegenerative diseases. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a fatal and multifactorial motor neurodegenerative disorder, is characterized by oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and metal dyshomeostasis, providing a strong rationale for exploring boron-based therapeutics. This review examines current literature on B chemistry, pharmacology, and translational applications, with emphasis on mechanisms relevant to ALS pathogenesis. This review focuses on ROS-responsive B scaffolds, blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability, neuroprotective mechanisms, hormonal modulation, metal chelation, and emerging preclinical evidence supporting boron-based interventions. BCCs represent a promising yet underexplored therapeutic platform for ALS and related neurodegenerative disorders. Their ROS-responsive, redox-modulating, and neuroprotective properties, combined with favorable CNS drug-like pharmacokinetics, offer a mechanistically distinct approach to disease modification. Emerging preclinical evidence strongly supports further translational investigation.

articles.title: Ventral Lung Injury and Pneumothorax in Patients With Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Receiving Long-term Positive Pressure Ventilation.
A phase II, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of cannabis extract for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: the EMERALD trial.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with limited disease-modifying treatment options. Preclinical and clinical data suggest that cannabinoid-based therapies may exert neuroprotective and symptomatic benefits. We conducted a trial to evaluate the effects of cannabis-based medicine extract (CBME) on disease progression in patients with ALS. This was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Participants received CBME or placebo for 6 months. The primary outcome was the difference in ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) scores at the end of treatment (EOT). Secondary outcomes included adverse events, forced vital capacity (FVC), pain and spasticity measures, weight loss, cognition and quality of life. Due to COVID-19 restrictions and driving limitations, only 17 participants were enrolled (CBME: n=8; placebo: n=9), and 8 completed treatment (4 per group). At EOT, adjusted mean ALSFRS-R scores were 31.67 for CBME and 34.33 for placebo (difference: -2.66; 95% CI -7.25 to 1.92; p=0.18; n=8). No significant differences were observed in secondary outcomes. Post hoc analyses suggested potential effects of CBME on pain and cognition for further confirmation: usual pain intensity decreased by 2.52 points (95% CI -8.92 to 3.87, p=0.34; n=8), a decrease of 3 days in the number of pain days (95% CI -28.90 to 22.59, p=0.75; n=8), executive function improved by 7.71 points (95% CI 0.90 to 14.52; p=0.04; n=8) and a 5.68-point improvement in memory (95% CI -0.29 to 11.64; p=0.06; n=8). This trial did not achieve the target sample size therefore was underpowered to demonstrate efficacy of cannabis in slowing ALS progression. However, exploratory analyses generated hypotheses regarding possible effects on pain and cognition which require confirmation in adequately powered studies. (ID: NCT03690791) on 27 September 2018.

articles.title: From technique to sensitivity: the transformation of clinical and ethical reasoning in physiotherapy students in the context of chronic neurodegenerative diseases.
articles.abstract: The evolution of Physiotherapy requires a shift from the biomedical model towards bioethical and humanistic approaches. This study explores how final-year students perceive their professional role when dealing with patients with complex neurodegenerative conditions, where traditional technical success is challenged by the irreversibility of the deterioration. Qualitative research based on interpretative description. Thirty final-year students from the University of Almería (Spain) took part, divided into five working groups. Three training sessions and discussions were held on Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), Alzheimer's disease, stroke and Rett syndrome. The data were analysed using thematic analysis and triangulation by researchers external to the study, with reflexivity ensured through logbooks. A shift in clinical reasoning was identified, with sensitivity taking precedence over technique. Students redefined therapeutic success in terms of "comfort" and support, valuing "microscopic achievements" such as the preservation of dignity and the alleviation of distress. Of particular note is the ability to adapt ethical principles according to the patient's cognitive integrity (autonomy in ALS versus protection in Alzheimer's) and the integration of the carer as an inseparable part of the therapeutic process. Future physiotherapists perceive humanization and the empathetic interpretation of non-verbal cues as essential therapeutic tools. Unlike previous studies focused on clinical experience, this research explores pre-clinical ethical maturation, offering a unique perspective on the educational foundation and humanistic predisposition of future graduates prior to their immersion in the healthcare system. It is imperative that academic curricula formally integrate competencies in bioethics, palliative care and emotional management to prepare graduates for extreme vulnerability and prevent early professional burnout.

articles.title: Molecular Mechanisms of Nanoparticle-Mediated Targeted Drug Delivery in Neurodegenerative Diseases.
articles.abstract: With global population aging, the incidence of neurodegenerative diseases continues to rise, and the blood-brain barrier (BBB) excludes approximately 98% of small-molecule drugs and nearly all large-molecule biologics from the central nervous system (CNS), so conventional small-molecule pharmacotherapy is largely limited to symptom modulation. Nanodrug delivery systems, including ligand-engineered polymeric, lipid, and inorganic nanoparticles as well as naturally secreted extracellular vesicles, have been proposed as a way to overcome the BBB and modulate disease pathways, and most of the supporting evidence currently derives from rodent models. This review synthesizes the molecular mechanisms by which these systems cross or bypass the BBB, summarizes representative disease-specific interventions in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and multiple sclerosis, and critically discusses translational bottlenecks, with the explicit aim of distinguishing established mechanisms from preclinical observations and clarifying the path to clinical investigation. We deliberately limited in scope to systems for which mechanistic and delivery data are available, and the rapid pace of the field means that conclusions about clinical efficacy cannot be drawn from the present preclinical literature. Nevertheless, it still provides valuable insights for research in this field.

articles.title: Neuronal cell-cycle re-entry stratifies clinical trajectories in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: The clinical heterogeneity of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) remains a fundamental barrier to effective therapy. While cell cycle re-entry in post-mitotic neurons is a known precursor to neurodegeneration, its role in defining patient-specific outcomes has never been established. Here, we integrate large-scale transcriptomic profiling from the AnswerALS cohort with mechanistic studies in human iPSC-derived spinal motor neurons to define how cell-cycle re-entry shapes disease heterogeneity in ALS. We identify a transcriptionally distinct patient subgroup with the highest expression of G1 or G2-phase cyclins that exhibit significantly slower functional decline (ALSFRS-R), whereas the engagement of S-phase markers correlates with accelerated disease progression. Nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction, a hallmark of ALS and related disorders, disrupts the spatial distribution of key regulatory proteins and may contribute to maladaptive cell-cycle activation. Our recent evidence suggests that impaired nuclear import may initiate, rather than merely accompany, neuronal cell-cycle re-entry. Using iPSC-derived motor neurons, we show that impaired nuclear import initiates TDP-43 pathology and global nuclear/cytoplasmic mis-localization of key ALS-related proteins. This nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction triggers a transient wave of cell-cycle activity immediately preceding neuronal cell death. Crucially, we show that DNA-replication initiation is a pathological inflection point of no return, as neurons entering S-phase accumulate replication-associated DNA damage and undergo cell death. Selective inhibition of CDK4/6 prevents S-phase entry and confers potent neuroprotection. Our findings demonstrate that impaired nuclear import drives maladaptive cell-cycle reactivation in ALS and that the depth of cell-cycle engagement stratifies neuronal fate and patient trajectories.

articles.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss.
articles.abstract: TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts 1-8 . Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

articles.title: Carbon dot-based nanomaterials in neurodegeneration: addressing neurobiological barriers and targeting challenges.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, represent a major global health challenge due to their progressive nature and limited therapeutic options. One of the primary obstacles to treating these disorders is the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which restricts the delivery of most therapeutic agents into the central nervous system. In recent years, carbon-based nanomaterials, particularly carbon dot (CD) nanostructures, have emerged as promising platforms for neurological applications owing to their ultrasmall size, BBB-crossing ability, and anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties, in addition to tunable surface chemistry, strong photoluminescence, and favorable biocompatibility. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent research developments in the application of CD-based nanomaterials, including carbon nanodots, carbon quantum dots, graphene quantum dots, and carbon polymer dots, for the potential treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. The synthesis strategies and carbonization approaches used to produce these carbon nanomaterials are discussed, along with their physicochemical properties relevant to neurobiological applications, such as particle size, surface functionalization, heteroatom doping, optical properties, and stability in biological environments. Furthermore, the mechanisms by which CD-based nanomaterials can traverse the BBB are examined, including receptor-mediated and adsorptive-mediated transcytosis pathways. In addition, their applications are discussed, with particular focus on their roles in bioimaging, biosensing, inhibition of pathological protein aggregation, antioxidative activity, and targeted drug delivery. Finally, key challenges related to toxicity, biodistribution, large-scale synthesis, and clinical translation are discussed, along with future perspectives for the development of multifunctional theranostic platforms. Overall, use of CD-based nanomaterials represents a promising emerging strategy for overcoming neurobiological barriers and enabling the development of next-generation nanotherapeutics for the management of neurodegenerative diseases.

articles.title: Impaired discrimination of negative facial emotions in pure motor ALS.
articles.abstract: Emotion recognition deficits in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) remain debated. We investigated whether patients with pure motor ALS (without cognitive and behavioural disturbances) and without clinically relevant mood disturbances are impaired in discriminating negative facial emotions, using a test without ceiling effects. This cross-sectional study included 35 patients with pure motor ALS, based on the revised Strong criteria and operationalised using the Edinburgh Cognitive and Behavioural ALS Screen (ECAS), without clinically relevant mood disturbances, alongside 35 age-, sex-, and education-matched cognitively and psychiatrically healthy controls. All participants completed a shortened five-emotion version of the Facial Emotion Intensity Rating Test - Congruent and Incongruent and the Facial Sex Matching Task (FSMT), a brief screening measure of non-emotional facial discrimination. Pure motor ALS patients showed poorer discrimination among negative facial emotions than healthy controls (p = 0.011, Cohen's d = 0.63). The group difference did not differ significantly across anger, fear, sadness, and disgust (p = 0.178). Similarly, the group difference in discrimination among negative emotions did not differ significantly from that in discrimination between negative emotions and happiness (p = 0.459). The two groups did not differ significantly on the FSMT. Discrimination of negative facial emotions was impaired in patients with pure motor ALS, suggesting that classification based on ECAS screening may underestimate social-cognitive involvement. Our findings are compatible with the concept of an ALS-frontotemporal spectrum disorder. Whether impaired emotion discrimination relates to additional cognitive or behavioural impairment remains to be determined. The clinical utility and reliability of our measure require further study.

articles.title: Lower frequency ECoG features improve longitudinal stability of speech and hand-grasp detection in a patient with progressive ALS.
articles.abstract: Achieving long-term decoding stability is a critical challenge for chronicintracranial brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). High-gamma (HG) activity fromintracranial recordings is the standard signal for BCI control, and lower-frequency featurescan enhance HG decoding performance. This study evaluated the longitudinal stability ofspeech and hand-grasp detection models using individual and joint spectral features, andthe local motor potential (LMP).Approach. Longitudinal data from a single participant implanted with two 64-channelECoG arrays were used to evaluate the long-term stability of logistic regression models forspeech and hand-grasp detection. Models were trained on individual frequency bands andon the LMP, a time-domain low-frequency feature, and evaluated over 21 months forspeech and 13 months for grasp. The best-performing band features were then combinedinto multi-band models and analyzed for their spatial contributions.Main Results. The LMP yielded the most accurate single feature models in both tasks(speech 93.8%, grasp 99.4%) and showed little or no decline. Multi-band modelscombining HG with lower frequency bands were substantially more stable than HG-onlymodels and outperformed the LMP models for speech but not grasp. HG accuracydegraded strongly for both tasks (speech:-4.3 percentage points per 100 days, or pp/100d,grasp:-3.4 pp/100d). HG+beta for speech showed a negligible decline (-0.5 pp/100d,95.6% ±0.06% overall), and for grasp, delta alone showed remarkable stability (+0.5pp/100d), while HG+beta+delta maintained 98.2 ±0.09% overall accuracy with flatperformance (+0.0 pp/100d). The advantage of the multi-band models increased overtime, reaching +20.6 pp for speech and +10.2 pp for grasp in the last 100 days.Significance. Incorporating lower-frequency neural activity yields more stable long-termspeech and grasp detection than HG alone. These findings indicate that lower-frequencyand multi-band features may reduce recalibration requirements for simple BCI tasks, andmay complement the precision control provided by HG activity.

articles.title: OGS-MA114 ameliorates FUS mutant-associated ALS pathology by activating PINK1-dependent mitophagy.
articles.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy are increasingly recognized as central contributors to pathogenesis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). In this study, we identified OGS-MA114 (C₂₃H₁₉ClN₄O₃S), as a compound that activates mitophagy through a bioactive chemical library screen in SH-SY5Y cells. OGS-MA114 significantly enhanced autophagic and mitophagic flux, increased Ser65-phosphorylated ubiquitin levels, and promoted Parkin recruitment to damaged mitochondria, indicating activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway. In SH-SY5Y cells expressing the ALS-associated FUS P525L mutant, OGS-MA114 restored mitochondrial membrane potential, reduced cleaved caspase-3 levels, and improved cell viability under mitochondrial stress conditions. Furthermore, in a transgenic zebrafish model expressing mutant FUS R521C , OGS-MA114 significantly improved locomotor activity and survival while reducing cell death in the spinal cord. These findings suggest that OGS-MA114 ameliorates ALS-associated pathological phenotypes by enhancing PINK1-dependent mitophagy. Thus, pharmacological modulation of mitophagy may provide a useful basis for further investigation of ALS and -related neurodegenerative disorders.

articles.title: The neuro-inflammaging triangle: a self-amplifying circuit of protein pathology, senescence-associated secretory phenotype and innate immunity in neurodegenerative disease.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, share common pathological features, including abnormal protein aggregation, chronic neuroinflammation and progressive neuronal loss. Ageing is the strongest risk factor, accompanied by a chronic, mild inflammatory state called 'inflammaging,' partly due to senescent cells producing senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors. Innate immune DNA- and danger-sensing pathways, most notably the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway and NOD-like receptor family, pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasomes, convert cellular injury into chronic neuroinflammation. Here, we propose that protein pathology, SASP, and innate immune activation form a self-amplifying triangular circuit leading to age-related neurodegeneration. We present the cellular and molecular basis of each part and how microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells and neurons contribute. We outline treatment strategies, including senolytics, senomorphics, innate immune pathway inhibitors and metabolic restoration, and identify unresolved questions, including the reversibility of post-mitotic neuronal senescence, the relative contribution of each cell type and the translational challenge of interrupting the cycle. Collectively, the neuro-inflammaging triangle theory shifts focus from individual pathogenic entities to the self-amplifying circuit that sustains them, offering a unified mechanistic model to advance our understanding and treatment of age-related neurodegeneration.

articles.title: Therapeutic Potential of Liposomes in Targeting Neurodegenerative Diseases: Mechanistic Insights and a Future Perspective.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, are progressive disorders with limited disease-modifying treatments. Poor drug bioavailability, systemic toxicity, and restricted Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB) penetration remain major therapeutic challenges. Although previous reviews have discussed liposomal delivery, an updated mechanistic and translational assessment is needed. This review analyzed relevant studies on liposome-based drug delivery for neurodegenerative diseases, focusing on BBB penetration, targeting strategies, formulation characteristics, therapeutic mechanisms, and translational challenges. Liposomes improve drug solubility, stability, bioavailability, and brain delivery through passive transport, receptor-mediated transcytosis, adsorptive-mediated transport, and ligandassisted targeting. Functionalization with transferrin, lactoferrin, peptides, antibodies, and other ligands can enhance BBB transport and site-specific delivery. Liposomal systems target key pathological mechanisms, including amyloid-β aggregation, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and dopaminergic neuronal degeneration. Major gaps include limited clinical validation, long-term safety data, BBB-targeting efficiency, formulation stability, and manufacturing scalability. Compared with earlier reviews, this review integrates recent advances in liposome engineering with disease-specific mechanisms, BBB-targeting strategies, therapeutic outcomes, and translational barriers, providing a comprehensive perspective on the progression from preclinical development toward clinical application. Liposomes represent a promising platform for targeted therapy of neurodegenerative diseases. Standardized evaluation, scalable manufacturing, long-term safety assessment, and well-designed clinical trials are essential for establishing their therapeutic efficacy and facilitating clinical translation.

articles.title: TNIP1 acts as an aggrephagy receptor that assembles clearance machinery for protein aggregate removal.
articles.abstract: Selective autophagy receptors recognize and recruit harmful intracellular components to autophagosomes for degradation, and their dysfunction is linked to neurodegeneration, metabolic disorders, and cancer. Here, we identified TNFAIP3 interacting protein 1 (TNIP1) as an aggrephagy receptor implicated in neurodegenerative diseases. TNIP1 accumulated at polyubiquitinated protein aggregates upon proteotoxic stress. Genetic depletion of TNIP1 reduced protein aggregate clearance and increased axonal degeneration under proteotoxic stress. Mechanistically, TNIP1 enhanced protein aggregate clearance by assembling aggrephagy receptors, such as SQSTM1/p62 and TAX1BP1, onto protein aggregates. Gene expression analysis revealed that TNIP1 expression levels are reduced in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) with TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) inclusion pathology. Additionally, an ALS-associated TNIP1 mutant exhibited impaired association with TDP-43 aggregates and failed to rescue their autophagy-mediated degradation. These findings establish TNIP1 as an aggrephagy receptor and reveal its potential role as a therapeutic target for ALS and other proteinopathies.

articles.title: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis treated with the modified Bu-Shen-Jian-Pi decoction (mBSJP): Multicenter study.
articles.abstract: To investigate whether the modified Bu-Shen-Jian-Pi decoction (mBSJP) is more efficacious than the hitherto used and promoted BSJP formula in the treatment of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). ALS is a fatal neurodegenerative disease with no satisfactory treatment option. Currently, there are few palliative care methods that can significantly delay the progression of the disease, and the efficacy of the herbal treatments used hitherto has also been unsatisfactory. A total of 165 patients with ALS who met the diagnostic criteria after screening were randomly allocated into two groups, a modified Bu-Shen-Jian-Pi decoction group referred to as the mBSJP group and the placebo group. Clinical efficacy and side effects were evaluated during a 16-week observation period. Primary outcomes included Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Symptom Score in Integrative Treatment Scale (ALS-SSIT) and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) scores, and secondary observation parameters were 36-Item Short-Form Health Survey Questionnaire (SF-36) and forced vital capacity (FVC). A total of 73 patients in the mBSJP group and 71 patients in the placebo group completed the trial. At the end of the 16 th week of treatment, there were significant statistical differences observed between the two groups in values for both the ALS-SSIT and the ALSFRS-R scores showing that mBSJP significantly delayed progression of the disease and appearance of symptoms compared to the administration of placebo. Treatment of ALS with mBSJP delays disease progression and is recommended as a treatment option for ALS in regions where the use of traditional Chinese medicine is regulated and approved.
articles.journal: International journal of clinical pharmacology and therapeutics

articles.title: Beyond Motor Neuron Degeneration: Non-Motor Manifestations and Multisystem Involvement in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that primarily affects the motor system through the degeneration of motor neurons in the motor cortex, brainstem nuclei, and anterior horn of the spinal cord. ALS typically has a focal onset characterized by muscle weakness, followed by progressive spreading to other body regions, with respiratory muscle failure representing the main life-limiting complication. Median survival is approximately 2-5 years after disease onset. In addition to the well-established motor manifestations, non-motor symptoms are increasingly recognized and may occur in approximately 50% of patients. These include behavioral and neuropsychiatric disturbances, sleep disorders, sensory abnormalities, autonomic dysfunction involving the cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary systems, as well as metabolic and endocrine alterations. Recent evidence supports the concept of ALS as a multisystem disorder characterized by substantial clinical, genetic, and neuropathological heterogeneity. Nevertheless, non-motor manifestations remain less extensively characterized than motor symptoms and are frequently underestimated in clinical practice. This narrative review summarizes the current evidence on non-motor manifestations in ALS, discusses their potential underlying mechanisms and impact on quality of life, and highlights areas requiring further investigation. A better understanding and systematic assessment of these manifestations may contribute to a more comprehensive and patient-centered approach to ALS care.

articles.title: Beyond neurones: cardiac involvement in motor neurone disease.
articles.abstract: Motor neurone disease (MND) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder defined by the progressive loss of upper and lower motor neurones. This degeneration leads to muscle wasting and weakness, most prominently affecting the upper and lower limbs, the bulbar musculature responsible for speech and swallowing, as well as the respiratory muscles (Feldman et al., 2022). As the disease advances, affected individuals experience profound functional decline, loss of independence, and ultimately respiratory failure, which remains the leading cause of death (Kiernan et al., 2021). Despite advances in understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms of MND, effective disease‑modifying treatments are limited and there is no cure. Management therefore focuses largely on symptomatic treatment and multidisciplinary supportive care to maintain quality of life (Simon et al., 2015). The long-standing view of MND as a disease confined to the motor system is increasingly being challenged. Emerging evidence from human and rodent studies suggests that other organ systems, such as the heart, may also be affected, raising the possibility that cardiac involvement is a clinically relevant but under‑recognised feature of the disease.
